title: Writ Remedies against Administrative Action — Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Certiorari, Prohibition and Quo Warranto

content.overview: Writ remedies are the principal constitutional tools for controlling administrative action. Under Articles 32 and 226 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court and High Courts may issue habeas corpus, mandamus, certiorari, prohibition and quo warranto to protect rights and keep public authorities within legal bounds. Choice of writ depends on the nature of the grievance and the relief sought.
content.glance: Identify the right or legal duty engaged, the public authority and the defect in its action, then match the appropriate writ: habeas corpus (liberty), mandamus (enforce duty), certiorari (quash), prohibition (stop excess), quo warranto (challenge office).
content.study:
Constitutional foundation: Article 32 guarantees the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of fundamental rights. Article 226 empowers High Courts to issue writs for enforcement of fundamental rights and for any other purpose. High Court jurisdiction under Article 226 is wider in subject-matter than Article 32.

Habeas corpus: Commands production of a person alleged to be unlawfully detained and inquiry into the legality of detention. It is the primary remedy for personal liberty.

Mandamus: Commands a public authority to perform a public duty that it has failed or refused to perform. It does not ordinarily compel exercise of pure discretion in a particular way, but can require that a duty be performed according to law.

Certiorari: Quashes an order or decision of a judicial, quasi-judicial or, in appropriate cases, administrative authority that has acted without jurisdiction, in excess of jurisdiction, or in violation of natural justice or the law.

Prohibition: Restrains an authority from continuing proceedings that are in excess of jurisdiction. It is preventive; certiorari is corrective.

Quo warranto: Challenges a person's claim to a public office. It asks by what authority the office is held and can lead to ouster if the appointment is unlawful.

Maintainability: Standing, alternative remedy, delay and the public-law character of the duty or decision affect whether a writ will issue. Writ jurisdiction is discretionary and equitable in character under Article 226.

Current-law framing: Ground the analysis in Articles 32 and 226 and in the specific statute creating the duty or power under challenge. Do not treat the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 as the source of writ doctrine; evidence provisions apply only when proof issues arise.

sections.heading: Constitutional Foundation
sections.body: Article 32 is the constitutional remedy for enforcement of fundamental rights in the Supreme Court. Article 226 empowers High Courts to issue writs for fundamental rights and for any other purpose, giving them broader subject-matter reach. Both jurisdictions are supervisory tools over public power.

sections.heading: Habeas Corpus
sections.body: Habeas corpus secures personal liberty by requiring production of the detained person and examination of the legality of detention. Unlawful detention, including detention in excess of legal authority or in breach of mandatory safeguards, can be corrected by this writ.

sections.heading: Mandamus
sections.body: Mandamus enforces performance of a public duty. The applicant must show a clear legal right to the performance of the duty and a corresponding duty on the authority. It is not a tool to dictate the manner of exercising pure discretion in a particular way, but it can compel action according to law.

sections.heading: Certiorari and Prohibition
sections.body: Certiorari quashes a decision already made without or in excess of jurisdiction or in breach of natural justice or law. Prohibition restrains an authority from continuing proceedings that exceed jurisdiction. Certiorari is corrective; prohibition is preventive.

sections.heading: Quo Warranto and Maintainability
sections.body: Quo warranto tests the legal authority by which a person holds a public office. Across all writs, courts consider standing, alternative remedies, delay and the public character of the duty or decision when deciding whether to grant relief.

examples.title: Unlawful detention
examples.body: A person is detained under an order that fails mandatory statutory safeguards. The appropriate writ is habeas corpus to test the legality of detention and secure release if the detention is unlawful.

examples.title: Refusal to perform a public duty
examples.body: A statute requires an authority to process and decide applications of a stated class within a framework. The authority refuses to consider an eligible application at all. Mandamus may issue to compel performance of the duty according to law.

examples.title: Order without jurisdiction
examples.body: A tribunal passes a final order on a matter outside its statutory jurisdiction. Certiorari is the appropriate writ to quash the order. If proceedings are still pending and excess of jurisdiction is clear, prohibition may restrain continuation.

hypotheticals.question: Can mandamus force an authority to exercise discretion in a particular way?
hypotheticals.analysis: Ordinarily no. Mandamus can compel performance of a public duty and require that discretion be exercised according to law, but it does not usually dictate the particular outcome of a true discretionary choice.

hypotheticals.question: When is certiorari preferred over prohibition?
hypotheticals.analysis: Certiorari quashes a decision already made. Prohibition restrains ongoing or threatened proceedings in excess of jurisdiction. Choose according to whether the impugned action is complete or still in progress.

distinctions.title: Certiorari vs prohibition
distinctions.left: Certiorari quashes a decision already made.
distinctions.right: Prohibition restrains an authority from continuing excess-of-jurisdiction proceedings.

rows.right: During or before continuation of proceedings.
Preventive — stops further action in excess of jurisdiction.

distinctions.title: Article 32 vs Article 226
distinctions.left: Article 32 is confined to enforcement of fundamental rights in the Supreme Court.
distinctions.right: Article 226 covers fundamental rights and any other purpose in the High Courts.

rows.right: Fundamental rights and other legal rights/duties (wider).

misconceptions.trap: Every administrative grievance automatically attracts a writ.
misconceptions.correction: Writ relief is discretionary; standing, alternative remedy, delay and public-law character of the duty matter.

misconceptions.trap: Mandamus can always dictate the particular exercise of discretion.
misconceptions.correction: Mandamus enforces public duties and lawful exercise of power; it does not ordinarily substitute the court's preferred discretionary outcome.

misconceptions.trap: BSA provisions define when writs issue.
misconceptions.correction: Writ jurisdiction arises from Articles 32 and 226; evidence law is relevant only to evidentiary questions.

cases.name: Tata Cellular v Union of India
cases.facts: The case concerned judicial review of administrative decision-making in a governmental contractual and commercial context.
cases.issue: What is the scope of judicial review and the limits on court intervention in administrative action?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Court articulated limits on judicial review, emphasising legality and rationality of the decision-making process rather than substitution of commercial judgment.
cases.holding: The Court applied those review standards to the administrative decision under challenge.
cases.relevance: Leading authority on the scope of judicial review that informs the use of writ remedies against administrative action.

cases.name: State of Uttar Pradesh v Maharaja Dharmander Prasad Singh
cases.facts: The case concerned the exercise of governmental power and the standards applicable to administrative action.
cases.issue: How should courts approach challenges to the exercise of administrative or governmental power?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Court examined the legal limits on the exercise of the power and the appropriate intensity of judicial review on the facts before it.
cases.holding: The Court disposed of the appeal by applying the governing legal standards to the administrative action under challenge.
cases.relevance: Authority already present in the topic file on review of administrative power; verification remains a separate gate.

cases.name: State of Tamil Nadu v P. Krishnamurthy
cases.facts: The case concerned challenges to subordinate legislation and the scope of judicial review over rule-making and related administrative power.
cases.issue: What grounds are available to challenge the validity of subordinate legislation and related exercises of power?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Court restated the established grounds on which subordinate legislation and related administrative action may be reviewed, including ultra vires and related legality defects.
cases.holding: The Court applied those grounds to the measure under challenge.
cases.relevance: Useful for the interface between writ review and challenges to delegated legislation; verification remains a separate gate.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a writ petition against administrative action be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Identify the right or public duty and the public authority. II. State the defect (jurisdictional, procedural, or substantive). III. Match the appropriate writ (habeas corpus, mandamus, certiorari, prohibition, quo warranto). IV. Address maintainability (standing, alternative remedy, delay). V. Formulate the precise prayer.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What should written submissions in a writ petition contain?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Set out facts and the public character of the duty or decision; identify the legal defect; justify the choice of writ; address alternative remedy and delay; and seek only the relief supported by Articles 32/226 and the record.
